analysis.one_liner: Restores federal brake requirements for trains carrying flammable oil and chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors; the Trump-era rule that dropped the brake mandate stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2018, the Department of Transportation repealed a requirement that trains hauling large amounts of oil or other flammable liquids use electronically controlled pneumatic brakes, which stop every car at once instead of one after another. H.R. 851 would have overturned that repeal and put the brake rule back into force. The bill never advanced beyond its committee referral, and the repeal remains the law of the road.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near rail lines that carry oil and other flammable liquids, and the emergency responders in those towns. The same trains have caused deadly runaway and derailment fires, and brakes that stop every car at once can cut stopping distance and keep derailed cars from jackknifing and piling up.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids the September 2018 DOT rule that removed the electronically controlled pneumatic brake requirement for high-hazard flammable unit trains and restores the prior regulations as if the repeal had never been issued.

The restored requirement applies to trains hauling large volumes of flammable liquids, the same traffic involved in catastrophic derailment fires such as Lac-Mégantic in 2013 and Mosier, Oregon in 2016.
The reinstated rule would take effect 90 days after enactment, giving railroads a short runway to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Railroads hauling oil and chemicals, and the oil and chemical shippers whose cargo moves over those rails, would bear the cost of installing and maintaining the electronically controlled brake systems. DOT's 2018 repeal cited those costs in dropping the rule; the industry had estimated the systems cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and DOT judged the proven safety gain too small to justify them.

drawbacks.text: DOT removed the brake rule after field testing and its own analysis found the systems added no proven safety benefit over improved conventional brakes on the trains most at risk, so reinstating the requirement imposes large costs for a benefit the department concluded was unproven.
Reinstating a rule by statute overrides the normal regulatory process, including the agency's cost-benefit judgment and its authority to update requirements based on new evidence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The brake requirement targets a real, documented hazard: mile-long trains of flammable liquids moving through towns. But the same technology was removed by the safety regulator itself after testing showed a limited benefit at high cost, and railroads had already upgraded track and tank cars under other post-2013 rules. The bill would lock in a costly mandate over the agency's contrary judgment; a more targeted fix would have had to pass the same committee that never acted on this one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its railroads subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler introduced the bill on January 29, 2019, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction, and on February 7, 2019 to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where the record ends.
No text, markup, floor action, or vote ever occurred, so the 2018 DOT rule removing the brake requirement was never challenged and remains in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads and the oil and chemical shippers whose cargo they haul, who are spared the cost of installing electronically controlled brake systems on flammable-unit trains, and who keep the 2018 deregulation in place.

for.name: Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; no cosponsor joined.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Peter DeFazio, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials subcommittee and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split is measurable.

industries.note: The bill would have forced railroads to install and maintain electronically controlled pneumatic brakes on trains hauling flammable liquids, a mandate DOT had dropped in 2018 partly on cost grounds. Because the bill died, railroads keep operating under the lighter 2018 rules; their savings come out of the safety margin of towns along the routes.

industries.industry: Crude oil producers and chemical shippers
industries.note: Shippers pay freight rates that absorb rail compliance costs, so the death of the bill preserves cheaper transport for high-hazard flammable cargo. The public interest runs the other way: these are the cargoes involved in the worst rail fire disasters.
